claims.text: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys can form amorphous states by melt-quenching.
These melt-quenched amorphous alloys may have limited thermal stability and crystallize upon heating.
Replacing 1–5 at% of a principal element with an isovalent metalloid such as silicon or boron will improve glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
The selected silicon or boron substitution can interact preferentially with phosphorus.
Metalloid substitution increases local atomic-size mismatch and atomic-packing frustration.
Greater heterogeneity in atomic sizes and bonding characteristics disrupts crystal nucleation.
The substitution introduces slight lattice distortions in the local atomic environment.
Preferential metalloid–phosphorus bonding and packing frustration raise the kinetic barrier to atomic rearrangements required for crystallization.
The raised kinetic barrier stabilizes the amorphous phase during cooling and subsequent thermal cycling.
Relative to an otherwise comparable unsubstituted alloy, the substituted alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate.
Relative to an otherwise comparable unsubstituted alloy, the substituted alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature.
The intervention should work only at substitution levels low enough not to dominate the alloy's mixing enthalpy or substantially alter its overall composition.
The benefit will diminish if the substitution level is excessive.
The benefit will diminish if the metalloid does not interact favorably with phosphorus or adequately modify the local bonding environment.
A 3 at% substitution can be tested against an unmodified control using DSC, critical-cooling-rate measurements, and XRD.
